name: Story — Amberworks
html:
Amberworks is a lighting studio built on collaboration between artisans, materials, environments, and the community around us.

Working together, we're committed to reimagining the everyday, by pairing considered materials and unhurried craftsmanship with lighting built to outlast trend cycles.

Our founders, Marisol Reyes and Theo Lindqvist, are longtime collaborators whose path into business began with a shared instinct: to make well-designed objects that combined careful, made-to-order craftsmanship with manufacturing that could actually scale. With the launch of Amberworks in 2016, they introduced a distinct, systems-based design approach that still shapes much of the catalog.

name: Craft — Amberworks
html:
Craft & Collaboration

Marisol and Theo's respect for craft and materials goes back to early training in woodworking, metalsmithing, and textiles, long before either of them considered building a company together.

Today, that instinct shapes how we work. We start from the qualities native to each material — the way brass tarnishes, the way blown glass holds air — and let those tendencies guide the form a piece ultimately takes, down to the smallest, most quietly satisfying details.

On occasion, we've partnered with independent makers whose practice overlaps with ours, including glassblower Rosa Kettering and furniture designer Adrian Voss, to build small-batch collections that reflect a shared point of view.

We rely on a growing circle of craftspeople, engineers, and artists across the country who help bring our sketches into finished form. Every collaboration is a genuine partnership, with each maker helping shape a piece toward its most honest conclusion.

Our own backgrounds in fabrication let us take an especially hands-on approach with every partner, refining tooling and process together, sometimes over the course of years.

Whether you have a question about an order, a product, or would like more information about what we do, we'd love to hear from you. You can also explore our F.A.Q. for additional help.

name: FAQ — Amberworks
html:
Frequently Asked Questions

With proper care, our fixtures are designed to last for decades. Here's everything you need to know to choose the right piece for your project — and to keep ordering and care as simple as possible.

If you need more help, or have a question specific to your order, send us a note at hello@amberworks.co.

  • What materials do you work with?
  • Is there any variation in the materials?
  • Do you offer custom finishes?
  • Where are your products made?
  • Are bulbs included with each fixture?
  • Why do you use LED bulbs?
  • What certifications do your fixtures carry?
  • Can I customize the drop length of a pendant?
  • How can I request CAD, Sketchup, or Revit files?

As a rule, we only build with solid materials: brass, blackened steel, hand-blown glass, and stoneware. We favor manufacturing and finishing techniques that honor and reveal the character each material already has — and leave room for its natural variation.

Brass

All of our brass fixtures are left unlacquered and will patina naturally with time.

Steel

Our steel finishes are wet-coated for precise, lasting color, and as an economical alternative to powder-coating.

Glass

Our glass is either hand-blown or slumped over molds, and is often left with its naturally glossy finish intact.

Stoneware

Our ceramic components are slab-built, hand-thrown, or slip-cast, and left either raw or glazed to highlight the clay's natural texture.

name: Spotlight — Amberworks
html:
The Cinder Collection

Two experimental glassmaking techniques anchor this collection. The first applies finely milled glass powder to sheets of glass using traditional silkscreen tools, echoing how a printmaker layers ink onto paper. The result is a soft, textured surface that holds light the way paper holds pigment — dimensional, and marked by quiet variation.

name: Process — Planwerk
html:
The Planwerk process, step by step

Turning a used truck cover into a one-of-one piece takes longer than sewing something from a bolt of new fabric. Here's the short version.

  1. Spot the truck

    We track which covers are due to be retired long before they're cut down.

  2. Buy the cover

    Each one is bought whole, tarp and webbing together, straight off the truck.

  3. Wash and dry

    Every cover is washed to the same standard, then hung to dry for a full day.

  4. Mark the flaws

    A cutter walks the whole panel and marks the scuffs, tape marks, and holes to avoid.

  5. Cut the panels

    Panels are cut around the marked flaws, so no two bags ever share a layout.

  6. Stitch and reinforce

    Seams are double-stitched at every stress point, by hand, at our workshop.

  7. Quality pass

    Every finished piece is checked against the same list before it's allowed to ship.

  8. Ship as one

    Each bag ships with its own photo, because it's the only one that will ever look like it.

name: Story — Planwerk
html:
How it started

A lot has changed since two friends sewed a bag from a used truck cover in a rented garage. Here's roughly what happened.

1997

Two industrial design graduates start cutting bags from truck covers they buy directly off drivers outside the city.

2001

The first wholesale order lands — forty pieces, no two alike, shipped in the same week they were cut.

2008

The workshop moves out of the garage and into a converted print shop, still within walking distance of the original one.

2016

A repair bench opens alongside the cutting tables, because most of what breaks on a Planwerk is a seam, not the tarp.

name: Materials Cycle — Planwerk
html:
A loop, not a lifecycle

Most of what we use has already had one job. We try to make sure it gets at least one more after ours.

  • Source

    Retired truck covers, seatbelts, and inner tubes, bought directly from freight yards within 600km of the workshop.

  • Strip & wash

    Buckles and webbing are removed by hand and washed separately so nothing is lost to a bad cycle.

  • Build

    Panels become bags, straps become clips, and the offcuts become the smallest accessories we sell.

  • Return

    A bag that's done being a bag is taken back, stripped again, and the tarp starts its next loop.

Since 2019 we've kept the average distance between cover and cutting table under 600 kilometres, and we publish the number every year whether it goes up or down.

Frequently asked questions

How does a printed shoe actually fit?

Wearing a Solecast pair feels closer to a wetsuit than a sneaker. Because the lattice is grown from your own foot scan, pressure spreads evenly across the sole from the first step, with no dedicated break-in period.

How long does an order take?

Most pairs print, cure, and ship within seven days of your scan being confirmed. Limited collaborations and made-to-order colorways can take a little longer during a drop.

Can I return a pair that doesn't fit?

Yes. Every first order includes a 30-day fit guarantee — if the scan didn't translate the way you expected, we reprint or refund at no extra cost.

How do I submit a design as a creator?

Apply through the Designers page with a sketch or 3D file. Our team scores it for printability within two weeks and, if approved, lists it with no upfront cost to you.

name: Manifesto — Solecast
html:
To every shoe buyer

Over the last two decades we swapped film for sensors and paper letters for messages that arrive before we've finished typing them. So why does the shoe on your foot still come from a mold built for a stranger's average measurements?

3D printing has spent years knocking on the door of everyday life — prosthetics, prototypes, even entire houses have been printed before a pair of shoes ever left a factory line this way. What's been missing wasn't the technology. It was someone willing to point it at the thing people put on their feet every single morning.

At Solecast, we think that thing is footwear. Buying shoes still means guessing a size off a chart, walking them in for two weeks, and hoping a half-size up or down was the right call. We built a company to remove the guess entirely.

Picture an industry where any designer, anywhere, can publish a shape and have it produced only when someone actually wants a pair — no warehouse, no overstock, no shoes burned or buried because a season ended. That's the version of this business we're building toward.

Changing an industry isn't easy, but it's worth it.

Scan your feet, back a designer, or bring your own shape to the platform — every pair ordered funds another slot on our print floor.

name: FAQ — Tallbo
html:
Got a question? We're happy to help.

Tallbo spans a lot of ground — stores, delivery, assembly, and everything in between. Here are the questions our support team hears most often.

  • How long does delivery take?

    Most orders arrive within 5–9 business days. Larger case goods and made-to-order pieces can take up to four weeks; we'll show an estimate at checkout before you pay.

  • Do I need any tools to assemble my order?

    Every flat-pack piece ships with the fittings and a hex key you'll need. Larger wardrobes and bed frames go faster with a power drill, but it isn't required.

  • What's your return policy?

    Unused items in original packaging can be returned within 180 days for a full refund. Assembled furniture can be returned within 30 days if it's still in resalable condition.

  • Can I find a Tallbo store near me?

    We currently operate 312 stores across 41 countries. Use the store locator on our site to check opening hours and in-stock inventory before you visit.

  • Do you offer assembly service?

    Yes — our delivery partners can assemble most items on the spot for a flat fee, shown at checkout alongside your delivery options.

name: Brand Story — Tmrw

The concept

An archive built one season ahead

TMRW started in 2019, in the back of a converted auto shop in Long Beach, when three former running-shop buyers got tired of waiting for good gear to trickle down to the sale rack. What began as a sneaker consignment counter is now a full-line concept store, split evenly between our physical flagship and this site.

In store and online you'll find a working edit of the industry's most technical footwear brands — Asics, Saucony, New Balance, and On sit beside independent labels like Ferro Studio and Northline — alongside our own collections, a running drop calendar, and a club that meets every Sunday, rain or shine.

Made with more care

  • Made to Last

    Longevity is the most effective sustainability feature we know. The longer a jacket lasts, the smaller its footprint per year worn, so fit and repairability lead every design decision we make.

    We favor recycled and solvent-free fabrics where the performance holds up, and we keep testing new ones. Every material swap has to earn its place without giving up waterproofing.

  • Fair Production

    We work with a small number of factories we visit ourselves, audited against independent labor standards, so growth never gets ahead of how the people making our clothes are treated.

name: Featured Drop — Zeroseam
html:
Featured Drop

The Halcyon 3000

When you take a cult icon from 1994 and rebuild it in a single printed lattice, the result is impossible to ignore. Meet the Halcyon 3000 — a ground-up, 3D-printed reissue of the runner that first put us on the map. Coming full circle? We've only just started.

The structure is soft where it needs to give and rigid where it needs to hold, wrapped in a woven texture that echoes the original's ripple sole. The slip construction drops the laces entirely, so stepping in feels like the shoe was already warmed up for you.

It's less a sneaker than a small sculpture you happen to walk in. Built backward from the archive, printed forward into the future. The Halcyon 3000 is the clearest look yet at where a fused, seamless shoe can go — and this is only the first pair off the line.

name: Manifesto — Zeroseam
html:
A letter to everyone who wears shoes

In the last few decades we watched almost everything dematerialize: film gave way to sensors, mail gave way to inboxes, records gave way to streams. Strange, isn't it, that the thing we actually touch every day hasn't changed at all?

Software and media got the whole revolution. Content is instant, distribution is free, and yet the object in your hand still gets built the same way it did fifty years ago, then shipped across an ocean to reach you. Whatever happened to the promise that we'd eventually just print the things we need?

3D printing has always carried that promise, and we've watched the headlines for years — printed houses, printed limbs, even printed food. But it kept living in labs and hobby shops, never in anyone's actual closet. So what is the one object stubborn enough, personal enough, and worn-out enough to finally carry printing into daily life?

At ZEROSEAM, we think it's shoes.

Old tooling, real frustration, and a basic human need to look like yourself: footwear has all three. And shoes are something literally everyone owns, which makes them the object most likely to teach an entire generation what a printed future actually looks like.

Picture a world where any designer, in any bedroom, can put out a real shoe with no factory minimum and no warehouse of unsold stock — while cutting into the mountain of pairs that get thrown out every single day. No glue seam to fail, no adhesive to break down in a landfill: just one fused material, made once, made to be worn.

None of this is simple. All of it is worth doing.

Come build it with us — reserve a production slot and your first pair.

Let's put it on the ground.

Mireille Okafor
ZEROSEAM, Co-Founder & CEO
